opening_message:
Ticket 1: Karen Alexander (employee ID E030) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E030.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Employee E030 (Karen Alexander) is a full-time Analyst. Requested write access to Source Code, which is at the maximum allowed level for full-time employees without owning-role admin. Recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E030 (Karen Alexander) is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors max out at read without advanced training; requested write exceeds max, so recommend read.
reason: HR records show E030 (Karen Alexander) is a full-time Analyst. Full-time employees may have up to write access, and admin only if their role owns the system; Analyst does not own Source Code (Engineer role does). The requested level (write) is at the maximum allowed, so write is granted. The security note's contractor classification conflicts with HR's authoritative employment record and its basic-training-based read cap does not apply to a full-time employee.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Karen Alexander (E030) requests write access to Source Code.

There are two notes from team memory:
- Note 1: HR says full-time Analyst, recommends write.
- Note 2: Security says contractor with basic security training, recommends read.

The two notes conflict on employment type. HR says full_time, Security says contractor.

Per policy:
- full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system.
- contractor: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

The conflict matters: if full-time, write is at max → grant write. If contractor with basic training, max is read → grant read.

Which source to trust? HR looked up in own database for role/employment type. Security looked up in own database for employment type and security training. Hmm.

The notes show conflicting facts. The Approver needs to make a decision. Typically, HR is the source of truth for employment type and role. Security is the source for security training. The security note says contractor with basic training, but HR says full-time.

Since HR is authoritative for employment type, Karen is a full-time Analyst. As full-time Analyst requesting write to Source Code: policy says full-time up to write; admin only if role owns system. Analyst doesn't own Source Code (Engineer owns Source Code). So maximum is write. Requested write → grant write.

Alternatively, should I consider the security note's employment type? The security DB might be outdated or wrong. The HR note says "looked up in own database" - both did. But HR is the authority for employment type.

I'll grant write.

Let me submit decision with reasoning.
